# Model: the argument infers causation from "wears less in cold + arthritis".
# The strongest challenge is a controlled counterexample: the supposed cause is
# present, the effect is absent, and background conditions (climate, city) match.
# An alternative-cause case (cause absent, effect present) only shows arthritis
# can have other causes. It does not refute that wearing less is a cause here.
# This is a rubric-based encoding of the logic, not a numeric proof.

options = {
    # cause_present, effect_present, same_background, supports_claim
    "A": dict(cause=True,  effect=False, same_bg=False, supports=False),  # different population (Japan); wording garbled
    "B": dict(cause=True,  effect=True,  same_bg=True,  supports=True),   # says wearing less makes attack easy -> supports
    "C": dict(cause=True,  effect=False, same_bg=True,  supports=False),  # sister, same city, same habit, no arthritis
    "D": dict(cause=False, effect=True,  same_bg=True,  supports=False),  # others with more clothes also get it
}

def undermine_score(o):
    if o["supports"]:
        return 0
    if o["cause"] and not o["effect"]:
        return 3 if o["same_bg"] else 2   # counterexample to sufficiency
    if (not o["cause"]) and o["effect"]:
        return 1                          # only an alternative cause exists
    return 0

scores = {k: undermine_score(v) for k, v in options.items()}
best = max(scores, key=scores.get)
ties = [k for k, s in scores.items() if s == scores[best]]

print("scores:", scores)
print("best option(s):", ties)
submitted = "D"
print("submitted:", submitted, "score:", scores[submitted])

if ties == [submitted]:
    print("CHECK PASS")
else:
    print("CHECK FAIL: expected", ties, "not", submitted)
